summary: The note surveys seasonal festivals and agricultural myths across four seasons in different regions: Harvest Sprites at the Autumn Equinox, the Cailleach at the Winter Solstice in Scotland, Les Demoiselles de la Saison at the Spring Equinox in France, and the Corn King's carnival at the Summer Solstice in the American Midwest. Each section features a local figure who keeps the tradition alive. It closes by reflecting that these festivals remain vital reminders of humanity's bond with the land and nature's cycles.
one_line: A tour of seasonal festivals and agricultural myths, from Harvest Sprites to the Cailleach, Maidens of the Season and the Corn King.
key_facts: The Autumn Equinox fell on September 23rd, 2023, and is linked to the agriculture fae, called Harvest Sprites by locals.
Farmer Ellie-May Thompson places miniature ornate scarecrows in her fields as an offering to the Harvest Sprites.
Village bard William Oakenleaf recites tales of dancing sprites at the Harvest Festival following the Equinox.
On the Winter Solstice, December 21st, 2023, villagers in the highlands of Scotland honor the Cailleach, a divine hag who rules the winter months.
Mythologist Aileen MacCrae shares legends that the Cailleach uses her staff to freeze the ground so the earth can rest before spring.
Lighting the Yule log is believed to encourage the Cailleach to be gentle with her wintry grip.
On the Spring Equinox, March 21st, 2024, a small French vineyard town celebrates Les Demoiselles de la Saison, the Maidens of the Season, who kiss grape buds to ensure a vintage year.
Vineyard owner JeanPierre Lefebvre dresses his young daughters in floral garlands to mimic the mythical maidens, and townsfolk perform the "Danse des Demoiselles".
On the Summer Solstice, June 21st, 2024, villagers in a remote American Midwest village wear costumes depicting the Corn King, a deity of crops, fertility, and abundance.
Artisan Mary Sanchez crafts the Corn King's mask yearly from harvested corn husks, vibrant feathers, and beads.
Children run through fields with sparklers mimicking fireflies, believed to be the Corn King's emissaries.
Stories say the Corn King battles blight and drought, with villagers' laughter bolstering his strength.
